title: The Options Market Says Adobe Stock Can Fall Over A Third Or Rise More Than Half
detail:
The Options Market Says Adobe Stock Can Fall Over A Third Or Rise More Than Half
Trefis Team
Mon, August 10, 2026 at 12:30 PM EDT 3 min read
ADBE
GOOG
CRM
ORCL
ORCL-PD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by Dx21 on Pixabay

Adobe has deliberately traded near-term recurring revenue for free users, and the option chain is charging for the uncertainty that leaves behind.

Adobe (ADBE) trades around $265 today, and the options market has already put a range on where the stock sits a year from now. The range is wide, and the company's own strategy is a large part of why: it has deliberately slowed its own recurring revenue to chase free users, and nobody yet knows what that trade returns. Owning the stock means owning that question.

A Floor Near $170 And A Ceiling Near $416 Both Count As Normal

The one-year chain, about 315 days out, prices at-the-money implied volatility at 48%. That maps to a two-in-three range from a floor near $170 to a ceiling near $416, roughly 36% below today's price and 57% above it. Neither end is a forecast or a boundary: there is about a one-in-six chance of finishing outside each one.

On a $10,000 position, that is roughly $3,600 of loss at the low end of that band against roughly $5,700 of room at the high end. A fall of that size needs a larger percentage gain to undo it, and this arithmetic is what the Trefis High Quality Portfolio is built around.

Why The Priced Range Is Wider Than Adobe's Own Record

Over the trailing year the stock's realized volatility, what it has actually delivered, was 38.5%, and the options market is quoting 48.4%, or 1.26 times as much. A broad reading of Adobe's implied volatility sits in the 92nd percentile of its own trailing one-year range. The market is not extrapolating this stock's history. It is pricing a change.

Much of that change is Adobe's own choice. Rather than push its record traffic into paid journeys, the company is routing it into the free Firefly and Express funnels, and it deferred the price step-ups it had planned on Creative Cloud for fiscal 2026. Creative Freemium MAU went from 50 million to 90 million year over year, and Acrobat and Express MAU from more than 700 million to more than 850 million. Those users are not paying yet. One analyst has put the combined cost at roughly a half-billion-dollar adjustment to organic ARR, against a beginning book of business of $25.6 billion, and management's own timeline for the payoff runs into 2027.

Size The Position For A Print Near $170

None of this says the business is breaking. Revenue over the trailing twelve months is $25.2 billion, up 11.5% year over year at a 36% operating margin, so the width is not a solvency question. In fact, the market is paying a premium for protection: while the $420 call costs more in absolute dollars ($13.50) than the $170 put ($7.68) due to a stock's mathematically unbounded upside, adjusting for this baseline reveals that downside puts are actually priced richer than upside calls.

Intel's $15 billion stock sale dilutes shareholders but avoids more debt as its 2026 capital spending forecast climbs above $20 billion.

Oracle shares fell 9% and Google turned free cash flow negative for the first time as AI infrastructure costs alarm investors across the sector.

Intel must prove AI investments generate returns above capital cost, or shareholders will have financed the boom while owning less of the company.

Don't wait: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just revealed his top 10 AI stocks. See the full list FREE now.

The AI boom is creating an unusual problem for investors: The companies spending the most to build the infrastructure behind it are increasingly being asked to prove that the spending will produce returns. 

Shutterstock

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) has pursued an $84.75 billion equity raise, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has turned to both debt and equity to fund its data-center expansion, and the five largest U.S. AI data-center builders have added roughly $350 billion of debt over five years, according to Bloomberg data reported by the Los Angeles Times. 

Now Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) is adding another wrinkle. It isn't borrowing $15 billion. It's selling stock.

Intel Is Choosing Dilution Over More Debt

Intel announced this morning that it plans to raise $15 billion through a public offering of common stock, with underwriters also receiving an option to purchase another $2.25 billion. The company said the proceeds will support general corporate purposes, including capital expenditures and working capital, as it expands to meet demand tied to AI compute and semiconductor manufacturing. The Wall Street Journal reported that Intel has already raised its 2026 capital-expenditure forecast from $18 billion to more than $20 billion.

The market's response was immediate: Intel shares are down more than 3% in morning trading today.

Let's be clear about what shareholders are seeing. Debt creates interest expense. Stock issuance creates dilution. Intel is effectively telling investors it would rather increase its share count than pile even more debt onto the balance sheet.

That's not necessarily the wrong decision. Intel issued $6.5 billion of senior notes in April, including bonds carrying coupons ranging from 4.65% to 6.20%. But shareholders still pay a price.

The only fresh operating news of the week does not come online for another two years.

CoreWeave (CRWV) stock rose 26% over the week to Friday, while the S&P 500 gained 3.5% and none of the peers listed here came close: MSFT 7.6%, AMZN 1.1%, GOOGL -0.5%. A gain that size usually follows new information, even in a stock this volatile. This one mostly anticipated it: the company has not reported yet, and the one operating announcement inside the week changes nothing about the question the report has to answer.

The Only Operating News Was 360 Megawatts, Two Years Out

The one fresh operating development announced during the week was an expansion into Indonesia, the company's first data center presence in the Asia-Pacific region: three new facilities totaling 360 megawatts of contracted IT power, expected to come online in 2028. Set against the more than 3.5 gigawatts of contracted power CoreWeave already held at the end of Q1 2026, that is roughly a tenth more footprint, two years out. Good news. Not a 26% event.

Demand Was Never CoreWeave's Bottleneck

Contracted revenue backlog stood at $99.4 billion at the end of Q1 2026 against $6.23 billion of revenue over the trailing twelve months, and orders are still arriving: days before the run began, Flow Traders picked CoreWeave as the primary AI cloud platform provider for its AI and deep learning division. The unproven half is conversion, and by management's own account it front-loads cost ahead of revenue. A powered shell arrives; lease, power and depreciation start running; and on average about one to two months of fit-out pass before a single dollar can be billed. That is part of the mechanism behind a -2.6% operating margin against a three-year average of 7.2%, with that current figure measured across the trailing twelve months. The 23-point gap between that operating margin and a -26% net margin represents roughly $1.43 billion in trailing-twelve-month costs, driven predominantly by interest expense, which hit $536 million in Q1 2026 alone. That funding load is the sort of strain the Trefis High Quality Portfolio's holdings tend not to carry, and their balance-sheet strength is what got that portfolio through past market storms.

The Week Priced The Event, Not The Results

The Q2 2026 report is due after Tuesday's close, and options traders were already braced for a swing of about 15.5% around it. A stock whose recent tape includes an 11.4% fall on one late-July session and a 22% gain on another is not saying much by rising 26% in a week. The run still leaves the stock about 39% below its 52-week high of $148.75; a 26% week does not undo that. The other disclosure from the same week has nothing to do with capacity: the chief executive sold $28.2 million of stock into the rally. That is a fact about one seller's timing, not about the quarter, and it leaves the week's operating news where it started: 360 megawatts for 2028. If the question is whether to hold through the print, the honest input is not last week's direction but the size of the move the options market is already charging you for.

Enjoy The Move, Then Check What It Did To Your Allocation

A move like this is even better to own than to watch, and it is also how one holding grows into an outsized share of a portfolio. Either way, a position that has grown large enough to matter is worth sizing deliberately rather than by accident. It's been a wild ride for AI stocks this summer. And it's easy to get startled at the first signs of heightened volatility. Anirudha Bhagat

Trading disclosure

Salesforce Inc. CRM has had a difficult year. The stock has fallen 17.2% over the past 12 months, significantly underperforming the Zacks Computer and Technology sector, which has gained 31.7% during the same period.

However, Salesforce is not alone. Other major software companies, including Adobe Inc. ADBE, SAP SE SAP and Oracle Corporation ORCL, have also faced strong selling pressure. Adobe, SAP and Oracle have declined 20.5%, 28.2% and 41.8%, respectively. This suggests that investors are questioning the outlook for the broader software industry rather than simply losing confidence in Salesforce.

Salesforce One-Year Price Return Performance
Zacks Investment Research


Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

AI Concerns Weigh on Salesforce Stock

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly agentic AI, is one of the biggest concerns facing software companies. AI agents can increasingly perform tasks with limited human involvement, raising questions about the traditional software-as-a-service model.

Investors are worried that companies could eventually need fewer software users as AI takes over more business processes. This could put pressure on subscription-based revenue models that charge customers based on the number of users.

The broader economy is adding to these concerns. High interest rates, inflation and geopolitical uncertainty have made businesses more careful about technology spending. Enterprises are taking longer to approve large software deals, creating longer sales cycles across the industry.

Salesforce is exposed to these challenges because its business depends heavily on large enterprise customers. Slower IT budgets could make it harder to win new customers and expand existing contracts.

Still, Salesforce's recent performance suggests that the company's core business remains resilient.

CRM's Revenue Growth Shows Signs of Stabilizing

Salesforce's slowing revenue growth has been a major concern for investors. As the company has grown larger, maintaining the rapid growth rates of its earlier years has naturally become more difficult.

Recent results, however, provide some reason for optimism.

First-quarter fiscal 2027 revenues increased 13.3% year over year. While this is well below Salesforce's earlier hypergrowth levels, double-digit growth is still meaningful for a company of its size.

Management expects double-digit revenue growth for the second quarter and full fiscal 2027. These forecasts are broadly aligned with Zacks Consensus Estimates.

Oracle's (NYSE: ORCL) stock has rallied 27% over the past two weeks. Let's see what catalysts drove its stock higher, and if it can maintain its momentum over the next few months.

Why did Oracle's stock soar?

The biggest catalyst for Oracle's stock was the expansion of its partnership with Alphabet's (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) Google on July 30. Google will integrate its advanced Gemini AI models into Oracle's AI Agent Studio, enabling Oracle's Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) customers to build and deploy AI agents with Google's AI software.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

OCI has been Oracle's primary growth engine over the past year. In fiscal 2026 (which ended on May 31), its cloud infrastructure revenue surged 77% to $18.1 billion, accounting for 27% of its top line, as more companies used its high-peformance GPU clusters to power AI applications.

OCI is much smaller than Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) Web Services (AWS), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Azure, and Google Cloud, but it integrates its services into those larger cloud infrastructure platforms so that its enterprise customers can run their workloads seamlessly across multiple cloud providers without being locked into a single ecosystem. Its expanded partnership with Google complements that strategy and increases its exposure to the AI market.

Another major catalyst was Microsoft's impressive earnings report on July 29. For fiscal 2026 (which ended on June 30), Azure's annual revenue surpassed $100 billion for the first time as Microsoft 365 Copilot reached more than 30 million paid seats. That robust growth suggests the AI supercycle -- which is driving most of Oracle's growth -- isn't slowing down. Lastly, hopes for milder macro headwinds drove more investors back toward higher-growth tech stocks.

Can Oracle maintain that momentum?

From fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2029, analysts expect Oracle's revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 39% and 30%, respectively. Those are incredible growth rates for a stock that trades at 22 times this year's earnings. Most of that growth should be fueled by OCI, which will directly profit from soaring AI workloads, its enterprise resource planning (ERP) services, and the growing usage of its cloud-based database services. All of those tailwinds should offset the ongoing decline of its on-premise software business -- which it's actively replacing with its cloud-based versions.

Michael Burry (Trades, Portfolio) is betting against Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS), sharpening his broader warning that the AI infrastructure boom is becoming dangerously dependent on leverage and long-dated financial commitments. The new shorts put two of the market's fastest-growing cloud infrastructure plays directly in the crosshairs of the investor famous for anticipating the U.S. housing crash.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with ORCL.

Is ORCL fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

Nebius is an Amsterdam-based AI cloud provider that rents Nvidia-powered computing capacity to companies building and running AI models. Its growth strategy requires enormous spending on GPUs, data centers and power infrastructure, making access to financing critical as it scales.

Burry disclosed a new Oracle short initiated at $144.63 per share, just days after closing his previous bearish position. That earlier trade consisted of January 2027 puts struck in the low $100s and generated what Burry described as a substantial profit.

He also shorted Nebius directly at $211.77, choosing shares instead of put options because option premiums were exorbitantly priced.

Oracle offers perhaps the clearest evidence behind Burry's leverage concerns. The company disclosed $260 billion of additional lease commitments, overwhelmingly tied to future data centers, that had not yet appeared on its balance sheet as of May 31. Capital expenditures surged to $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026, helping drive free cash flow to negative $23.7 billion.

However, Oracle's cloud infrastructure revenue surged 93% last quarter and remaining performance obligations reached $638 billion, giving bulls substantial contracted demand to point to.

Nebius presents a similar high-growth, high-capital-intensity debate. The company raised roughly $4.3 billion through convertible notes in March to finance data centers and GPUs, while signing a Meta infrastructure agreement potentially worth $27 billion. First-quarter revenue soared 684% to $399 million.

Investor Takeaway On Oracle Stock

Investors should watch whether contracted AI demand converts into cash quickly enough to justify the financing required to build capacity.

For Oracle, the key metrics are cloud growth, free cash flow, capital spending and its enormous future lease obligations. Its next earnings report is expected in mid-September.

For Nebius, utilization, customer concentration and additional funding requirements matter most. Rapid revenue growth would undermine Burry's bearish case; weaker demand, higher financing costs or delayed data-center deployments would strengthen it.
